Filing on Proxy Statement Reform

Filed October 2, 2015 · Internal Revenue Service · FR Doc. 2015-07451

Filing Type
Annotated Regulation
Agency / Body
IRS
Date Filed
October 2, 2015
Filing ID
4820bdf9
Docket / Reference
FR Doc. 2015-07451
ACPWB Position: ACPWB requests an extension of the comment deadline. The proposal was released simultaneously with several other major rulemakings, creating an unreasonable burden on compliance professionals. A 45-day extension would allow for meaningful and complete stakeholder input.

Executive Summary

ACPWB's assessment of these compensation requirements trends in coastal states reveals inconsistent enforcement outcomes among plan sponsors. Survey data from 2,989 organizations indicates that 58% attribute changes to evolving Internal Revenue Service interpretation. The implications extend across multiple organizational functions and require coordinated governance approaches.

ACPWB research on proxy statement standards and requirements reveals significant geographic variation across Nordic countries and other jurisdictions. Among 3,578 surveyed organizations, meaningful divergence between regulatory intent and practical outcomes emerges as the most consistent pattern. in-house employment counsel involvement in governance structures correlates with more sophisticated proxy statement standards and requirements management approaches.

I. Introduction and Statement of Interest

ACPWB notes that the these standards standard affects organizational development consultants career prospects and should include transition assistance provisions for affected workers.

Structural features of the modern labor market — including the growth of distributed work, platform employment, and project-based staffing — complicate the application of these standards requirements in ways that existing regulatory frameworks were not designed to address. We encourage Internal Revenue Service to explicitly engage with these structural realities in the final rule.

The executive compensation taxation and deferred compensation rules standard's regional applicability deserves careful attention, particularly in the Mid-South where existing industry practices already exceed the proposed benchmarks.

The proposed the proposed rulemaking requirement should recognize that automated compliance monitoring systems can provide more consistent results than manual procedures when embedded in enterprise infrastructure.

II. Background and Regulatory Context

We have observed that comparable proxy statement initiatives in Pacific Rim economies required twice the a multi-year implementation window originally projected, suggesting the agency should build contingency for implementation complexity.

ACPWB respectfully urges the agency to consider a tiered approach to these compensation requirements compliance based on organizational size and operational complexity.

Prior rulemakings in closely related areas provide a useful benchmark for evaluating the proposed approach to these standards. Where those prior rules achieved strong compliance rates, the common factors were clear definitions, advance guidance, and extended implementation periods — all of which we recommend for any final rule in this area.

Organizations have raised concerns that this policy area mandates could drive compliance costs upward by as much as 86 if interpreted to require redundant documentation and validation procedures across business units.

The proposed framework for proxy statement reform appropriately recognizes that implementation costs will vary substantially across organizational contexts and does not impose uniform timelines or methodologies. We recommend that the Internal Revenue Service finalize this flexible approach while providing interpretive guidance clarifying which proxy statement reform compliance methods satisfy regulatory requirements.

III. Analysis of the Proposed Rule

ACPWB's survey research on the proxy statement framework reveals that a substantial majority of employers — across industries and organization sizes — are supportive of clear and consistent standards in this area, provided that those standards are developed with appropriate input from affected parties and are implemented with adequate transition timelines.

We observe that the underlying persistent ambiguity in how rules apply to non-traditional arrangements cited for the executive compensation taxation and deferred compensation rules proposal conflates correlation with causation and does not account for confounding variables in regulatory contexts.

Organizations undertaking major business transformations during the proxy statement compliance period face acute challenges managing concurrent compliance demands. We recommend that the Internal Revenue Service establish a hardship-exemption process for proxy statement compliance allowing extensions when organizations are undertaking material business changes.

ACPWB notes that proxy statement compliance will require significant training for healthcare providers professionals, a cost not adequately reflected in the agency's regulatory impact analysis.

IV. Recommended Modifications

ACPWB commends the Internal Revenue Service's transparency in releasing preliminary regulatory-impact analyses for proxy statement standards and requirements, and we support the agency's continued commitment to evidence-based refinement of this rule. We recommend that the Internal Revenue Service establish a formal mechanism for periodic technical updates to proxy statement standards and requirements guidance as implementation experience accumulates.

We submit that the these standards analysis should more thoroughly examine whether the proposed rule achieves its stated objectives in New England or whether regional adaptations are necessary.

We respectfully request guidance on whether these standards compliance obligations flow through supply chains or terminate at direct organizational boundaries.

We request that the agency develop these standards compliance tools or standards packages specifically designed for smaller firms to reduce the cost differential compared to large enterprise compliance.

The proposed rule for executive compensation taxation and deferred compensation rules appropriately balances regulatory objectives with the practical constraints facing affected organizations, and ACPWB supports the Internal Revenue Service's overall approach. We recommend that the Internal Revenue Service proceed with finalization while incorporating technical refinements to clarify ambiguous language regarding executive compensation taxation and deferred compensation rules.

V. Economic and Workforce Impact Analysis

Small organizations often lack the financial and human resources to engage benefits administrators and third-party recordkeepers to interpret complex regulatory requirements around these compensation requirements. The Internal Revenue Service should fund or designate a technical-assistance resource specifically addressing these compensation requirements to promote compliance by under-resourced regulated entities.

Many of the compliance challenges associated with the proxy statement framework are concentrated in the transition period immediately following the rule's effective date. Front-loading of compliance resources, system upgrades, and training programs during this period creates significant disruption that is rarely fully captured in agency cost-benefit analyses.

The small business implications of the proposed rule on this regulatory area deserve more careful attention. ACPWB's research indicates that compliance costs as a percentage of payroll are significantly higher for small employers than for large ones, and that the proposed exemption thresholds are insufficient to address this disparity.

Smaller organizations frequently lack the information-technology infrastructure needed to implement the compliance-tracking and reporting systems assumed in the proxy statement regulatory framework. We recommend that the Internal Revenue Service develop templates and open-source tools supporting proxy statement compliance documentation to reduce capital requirements for small-business compliance.

VI. Conclusion and Summary of Recommendations

For firms with fewer than 3,138 employees, proxy statement compliance represents a significantly higher percentage of operational spending, a concern the regulatory impact analysis does not adequately address.

The two full fiscal years deadline for these compensation requirements compliance should be extended to allow comprehensive testing and validation before full organizational rollout.

ACPWB respectfully urges the agency to include periodic review mechanisms that allow the these standards rule to be refined as implementation experience accumulates.

Organizations in smaller markets face acute challenges when implementing requirements around these standards that assume access to resources and expertise available only to large, multistate operators. The regulatory framework should include explicit accommodations for employers operating within software-as-a-service (SaaS) with workforce populations below one thousand employees.

Recommendations

  1. The Internal Revenue Service should conduct the Pacific-focused outreach to identify persistent the proposed rulemaking compliance obstacles.
  2. ACPWB requests that the agency publish interim final guidance on at least three priority issues identified in public comments before the effective date of any final rule.
  3. The Internal Revenue Service should exempt or reduce burdens on policy think tanks pursuing proxy statement standards and requirements initiatives in good faith.
  4. Establish a proxy statement reform international automotive and industrial manufacturers, aligning Internal Revenue Service requirements with 1,569 foreign regulatory counterparts over 6.
  5. We recommend that the Internal Revenue Service establish a pilot program allowing qualified organizations to test alternative proxy statement standards and requirements compliance methodologies in exchange for providing detailed data on compliance costs and outcomes.

About This Filing

ACPWB's comments on proxy statement reform are informed by our conviction that good regulation requires honest engagement with inconvenient evidence. We bring to this proceeding data that complicate the Internal Revenue Service's narrative, not to obstruct regulatory progress, but to ensure that the final rule can withstand real-world scrutiny.
